Semiparametric models combine a finite-dimensional parameter with an unknown
function. The three principal `np` families differ in where that structure is
placed:

- `npplreg()` estimates $E(Y\mid X=x,Z=z)=x^\mathsf{T}\beta+g(z)$;
- `npindex()` estimates a link $g(x^\mathsf{T}\beta)$;
- `npscoef()` estimates $E(Y\mid X=x,Z=z)=\sum_j x_j\beta_j(z)$.

If you want a minimal downloadable script for the semiparametric route, start with [np_semiparametric_quickstart.R](www/np_npRmpi/np_semiparametric_quickstart.R).

LP-capable semiparametric families support joint degree-bandwidth search through
`nomad = "auto"`. For example:

```r
## Simulate a small partially linear example, then use the automatic LP shortcut.
## nomad = "auto" uses exhaustive search for p = 1 and NOMAD otherwise.
library(np)

set.seed(42)
n <- 200
x1 <- rnorm(n)
z <- runif(n)
y <- 1 + 2 * x1 + sin(2 * pi * z) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2)
dat <- data.frame(y, x1, z)

fit_pl_lp <- npplreg(y ~ x1 | z, data = dat,
  nomad = "auto", degree.max = 2L)
```

The same shortcut is available for supported `npindex()` and `npscoef()`
routes. It requires `crs`, which supplies the NOMAD runtime; `"auto"` uses
exhaustive search when there is one degree coordinate and NOMAD otherwise.

Use a semiparametric model when scientific structure supports one of these
restrictions and the remaining component should stay nonparametric.

## Partially linear models: `npplreg`

The partially linear model keeps the effect of $X$ linear while estimating
$g(z)$ nonparametrically.

In the `wage1` example, the idea is to treat some regressors parametrically while allowing experience to enter nonparametrically.

```r
## Keep some regressors linear while letting experience vary nonparametrically
library(np)
data(wage1, package = "np")

model_pl <- npplreg(lwage ~ female + married + educ + tenure | exper, data = wage1)

summary(model_pl)
```

Bandwidth selection for a partially linear model may be costly because its
criterion evaluates several cross-validated regressions.

`npplreg()` defaults to `se = FALSE`. Request `se = TRUE` when you need
`coef(model, se = TRUE)` or `vcov(model)`; the retained coefficient covariance
allows conditional heteroskedasticity. Prediction errors and asymptotic plots
request their required uncertainty separately.

## Single-index models: `npindex`

Single-index models reduce the nonparametric dimension from $x$ to the scalar
index $x^\mathsf{T}\beta$.

Two important routes are available in `np`:

- Klein-Spady style models for binary outcomes,
- Ichimura style models for continuous outcomes.

### Binary outcomes

```r
## Fit a binary single-index model on the mixed-data birthwt example
library(np)
data(birthwt, package = "MASS")

## Klein-Spady requires a numeric 0/1 response; predictors may be factors.
birthwt$smoke <- factor(birthwt$smoke)
birthwt$race <- factor(birthwt$race)
birthwt$ht <- factor(birthwt$ht)
birthwt$ui <- factor(birthwt$ui)
birthwt$ftv <- factor(birthwt$ftv)

model_index_binary <- npindex(low ~ smoke + race + ht + ui + ftv + age + lwt,
  method = "kleinspady",
  gradients = TRUE,
  data = birthwt)

summary(model_index_binary)
```

Current `np` and `npRmpi` releases retain the R model-matrix contrasts used for
factor predictors, so fitting, prediction, gradients, and plots share the same
single-index design. The Klein--Spady response itself must remain numeric `0/1`;
a factor response is rejected rather than silently interpreted through its
internal codes.

### Continuous outcomes

```r
## Use the continuous-outcome single-index route on wage data
library(np)
data(wage1, package = "np")

model_index_continuous <- npindex(lwage ~ female + married + educ + exper + tenure,
  data = wage1)

summary(model_index_continuous)
```

The single-index restriction reduces the dimension of the unknown link while
retaining a nonparametric response to the index.

### Interpreting and tuning the single index

`npindex()` is the one principal estimator that defaults to
`se = TRUE, se.type = "asymptotic"`, providing asymptotic coefficient covariance
and fitted-value standard errors. Set `se = FALSE` for a point-only fit when
that extra work is not needed. Selecting `se.type = "bootstrap"` uses
bootstrap resampling for fitted-value, gradient, and average-gradient errors;
coefficient covariance remains asymptotic in either mode.

With a local-constant uniform kernel, the link derivative is zero and cannot
provide covariance for free index coefficients. Use `se = FALSE` when only the
point estimate is required for that configuration.

The Ichimura and Klein-Spady objectives reuse the established `npreg`
leave-one-out backend where appropriate, and `npRmpi` distributes post-CV fit,
evaluation, and gradient work across evaluation rows. Fixed-bandwidth restarts,
nearest-neighbour metadata, objective certification, and retained formula data
are tightly validated.

Klein--Spady coefficient uncertainty conditionally centers the covariates on
the fitted index, so reported covariance is no longer sensitive to arbitrary
translations of the predictors. Coefficient-only refits retain the fitted
degree and bandwidth, avoiding another automatic degree or bandwidth search.

The coefficient vector is identified only up to scale, so `npindexbw()`
normalizes its first coefficient to one. Read the remaining coefficients as
relative movements in the index, not as standalone linear-model slopes, and
choose the first continuous regressor deliberately when coefficient
interpretation matters.

The default `optim.method = "Nelder-Mead"` remains a robust derivative-free
starting point for a low-dimensional search. For a higher-dimensional index,
`optim.method = "BFGS"` can be a useful performance and sensitivity
comparison. Because the objective can be nonconvex, compare objective values,
convergence behavior, and fitted objects rather than selecting an optimizer by
runtime alone.

## Varying coefficient models: `npscoef`

A varying-coefficient model lets each coefficient $\beta_j(z)$ change with the
conditioning variable $z$.

In the `wage1` illustration, coefficients are allowed to vary with sex.

```r
## Create numeric coefficient variables, then let them vary with sex
library(np)
data(wage1, package = "np")

wage1_augmented <- wage1
wage1_augmented$dfemale <- as.integer(wage1$female == "Male")
wage1_augmented$dmarried <- as.integer(wage1$married == "Notmarried")

model_scoef <- npscoef(lwage ~ dfemale + dmarried + educ + exper + tenure | female,
  betas = TRUE,
  data = wage1_augmented)

summary(model_scoef)
```

One practical detail matters: the `X` variables in the varying-coefficient part need to be numeric, so creating explicit `0/1` versions of factors can be appropriate there.

## Instrumental regression

The proof-of-concept `npregiv()` and `npregivderiv()` estimators now support
explicit formula/data interfaces. Use `y ~ z | w` for a response, endogenous
regressor, and instrument; `npregiv()` also supports `y ~ z | w | x` when
separate exogenous covariates are present. The returned objects have dedicated
summary, fitted-value, residual, gradient, and plot methods. Evaluation grids
are supplied during fitting rather than through post-fit prediction, and the
current IV estimators support fixed rather than nearest-neighbour bandwidths.

Start with the [instrumental-regression quickstart](www/np_npRmpi/np_instrumental_regression_quickstart.R).

## Hat and operator helpers

The public helper family now follows the estimator family directly:
`npreghat`, `npindexhat`, `npplreghat`, and `npscoefhat` cover regression and
semiparametric fits, while `npudenshat`, `npudisthat`, `npcdenshat`, and
`npcdisthat` cover density and distribution objects. These helpers can return
an explicit matrix, apply the operator without asking users to reconstruct it,
or produce the transposed response-weighted `output = "constraint"` form used
in constrained estimation.

`npreghat()` uses the canonical local-polynomial rank and bounded-ridge policy
shared by the hat, fit, objective, and bootstrap routes. Generalized-nearest-
neighbor and local-constant derivative ownership is validated explicitly. For
mixed polynomial degrees, available derivative components are routed through
the correct operator and unavailable components are reported explicitly rather
than silently applying a different derivative.

The constrained local-polynomial scripts in the [Code Catalog](code_catalog.qmd)
show the practical `npreghat()` workflow.

## How should I choose among these?

| If you want... | Start with |
|---|---|
| A mostly linear model with one clearly nonlinear part | `npplreg` |
| Dimension reduction through an unknown index | `npindex` |
| Coefficients that vary with another variable | `npscoef` |
| Maximum flexibility with fewer structural assumptions | `npreg` |
